title: OPEC+ Is About to Pause Oil Output Hikes. Here's What It Means for Oil Stocks. - The Globe and Mail
content: OPEC is unlikely to increase its output again this year. That could keep crude prices elevated as the market tries to rebuild global stockpiles. It could also affect Iraq's decision on whether to remain with the cartel. OPEC+ appears poised to pause its phased output increases after September. The group of OPEC members and several large oil-producing non-members have been steadily raising their collective output due to a severe supply shortage caused by the war with Iran. However, according to a Reuters report, it doesn’t plan to make any additional changes this year. Here’s a look at what this could mean for oil stocks. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Core members of OPEC+, which includes Saudia Arabia, Russia, and Iraq, will meet early next month to set their output target for September. The group expects to increase their production target by about 188,000 barrels per day (BPD) for September. That’s the same monthly increase as June, July, and August. OPEC+ members have been increasing their production quotas due to the impact of the war with Iran on the oil market. The September increase would mark the end of their phased rollback of a 1.65 million BPD supply cut that the group agreed to in 2023 to boost oil prices. They have been steadily increasing their collective production allotment this year to help offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz disruption on supplies. However, while OPEC+ has agreed to increase output, several members continue to struggle to get oil to the global market due to supply disruptions. For example, Iraq’s oil output has plunged from 4 million BPD before the war to around 1.4 million BPD. OPEC’s strategy of limiting member production has already led the UAE to leave the group this past May. Meanwhile, Iraq recently threatened to leave OPEC if it couldn’t increase its output. OPEC’s decision to maintain its production after September through the end of the year could hasten Iraq’s departure, especially if OPEC doesn’t boost its production quota for 2027. OPEC’s likely decision to pause additional output cuts could impact supplies later this year. The Strait of Hormuz has remained disrupted, forcing the oil market to burn through oil inventories and emergency stockpiles. The economy will eventually need to refill these shock absorbers, which could keep crude prices elevated. Goldman Sachs recently warned that oil could top $120 a barrel in the near term and average $100 next year if current disruptions persist. Higher oil prices would enable oil companies to make even more money. Another potential impact from OPEC’s decision is that it could ultimately drive Iraq to leave the group. That could have meaningful implications for several major oil companies. Chevron(NYSE:CVX) is working towards agreements to enter the Iraqi oil market. It recently signed memorandums of understanding with its government covering two oil fields, including the potential assumption of operational control over the large West Qurna 2, which alone accounts for 0.5% of global supply and 10% of Iraq’s output. Chevron is also considering a pipeline to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. If Iraq leaves OPEC or receives a meaningful increase in its production quota, it could enable Chevron to accelerate production growth in the country. Meanwhile, fellow U.S. oil giant ConocoPhillips(NYSE:COP) recently agreed to buy a 42% interest in BP Energy Company of Kirkuk. That investment will help support the ongoing development of four large-scale oil fields currently producing in the country. The fields hold an estimated 3 billion barrels of oil that the companies can recover through rehabilitation, redevelopment, and optimization activities. There’s also additional exploration potential. If Iraq can produce more oil in the future, it could enable ConocoPhillips and BP to invest more money and increase production more quickly. OPEC+ seems likely to pause any additional production increases after September. That could impact the oil market later this year as the global economy seeks to rebuild stockpiles caused by the current supply disruption. Meanwhile, it could have a longer-term impact if it drives Iraq to follow the UAE’s lead and leave the group. That would allow the country to increase production at will, potentially benefiting Chevron and ConocoPhillips. This potential catalyst makes OPEC’s future moves worth watching as it could have a meaningful impact on oil stocks. title: ExxonMobil's Q2 Earnings on Deck: Should You Bet on the Stock? - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM is set to report second-quarter 2026 results on July 31, before the opening bell. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for second-quarter earnings is pegged at $3.87 per share, implying a surge of almost 136% from the year-ago reported number. It has witnessed one downward estimate revision in the past seven days. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for second-quarter revenues is currently pegged at $95.8 billion, suggesting a roughly 18% rise from the year-ago actuals. XOM beat the consensus estimate for earnings in each of the trailing four quarters, with the average surprise being 6.04%. This is depicted in the graph below: Our proven model doesn’t predict an earnings beat for XOM this time around. The combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy), or 3 (Hold) increases the chances of an earnings beat. That isn’t the case here. The leading integrated energy player has an Earnings ESP of -2.40%. XOM currently carries a Zacks Rank #3. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. You can uncover the best stocks to buy or sell before they’re reported with our Earnings ESP Filter. In its latest 8-K SEC filings, XOM stated that it is likely to see a sequential improvement in the June quarter upstream earnings by $3.5 billion to $3.9 billion due to an increase in liquid prices. To have an idea of how oil prices behaved in the June quarter, let's analyze the commodity prices from the data provided by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (“EIA”). The average Cushing, OK, WTI spot prices for April, May and June of this year were $100.32 per barrel, $102.13 per barrel and $84.81 per barrel, respectively, per EIA data. Commodity prices were $63.54 per barrel, $62.17 per barrel and $68.17 per barrel, respectively, in April, May and June of 2025, according to the EIA. A constructive oil-price backdrop due to the Iran war aided the company’s exploration and production businesses in the June quarter of this year, similar to BP plc BP and Chevron Corporation CVX. XOM added that stronger margins from its Energy Products segment are likely to have provided a $2.0 billion to $2.4 billion sequential benefit. XOM's stock has jumped 37.2% over the past year, outperforming the industry’s 35.6% surge. BP has gained 28.4% over the same time frame, while Chevron has rallied 21%. While XOM’s stock price has outperformed the industry, the company appears relatively overvalued. The company's current trailing 12-month enterprise value/earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization (EV/EBITDA) is 10.23x, reflecting that it is trading at a premium compared with the industry average of 6.71x. Both BP and CVX are valued lower at 3.15x and 9.85x, respectively. ExxonMobil has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing lightweight proppant technology and hence is capable of boosting its well recoveries by up to as much as 20%. According to the data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, the shut-in price for existing wells in the Midland, a sub-basin of the Permian, is $42 per barrel. For Delaware, another sub-basin, the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas estimated the price at $34 per barrel. With West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude oil trading above the $80-per-barrel mark, significantly above the shut-in prices, it makes sense for XOM to continue production in the wells. Although the upstream business seems lucrative now, the high oil price is hurting the company’s refining operations, since the input costs have jumped. Also, with a significant proportion of earnings being generated from upstream activities, the company’s business is highly vulnerable to the volatility in commodity prices. Given the backdrop, it might not be wise for investors to bet on the integrated energy giant ahead of earnings because of its overvaluation. However, those who have already invested may hold on to the stock. The AI revolution has already minted millionaires. content: Chevron Corporation CVX is slated to release second-quarter 2026 results on July 31, before market open. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for revenues is pegged at $57.5 billion, implying an increase of 28.4% from the year-ago quarter. The consensus earnings mark of $5.81 per share has been revised upward by 1.8% over the past seven days, suggesting a 228.3% jump from the year-ago reported number. For full-year 2026, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for CVX’s revenues is pegged at $215.9 billion, implying an improvement of 14.2% year over year. The consensus mark for 2026 earnings per share stands at $15.60, indicating a surge of 114%. In the last reported quarter, the company delivered an earnings surprise of 53.3%. Chevron’s earnings beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate in each of the trailing four quarters, with the average surprise being 18.6%. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. Chevron's exploration and production business likely benefited from another quarter of solid production growth, supported by continued ramp-up across major assets. Management reaffirmed full-year 2026 production guidance of 3.98-4.10 million barrels of oil-equivalent per day (BOE/d), while highlighting that second-quarter production was expected to exceed the first quarter despite planned maintenance. Operations at TCO were running above 1 million BOE/d day, Gorgon and Wheatstone LNG were operating at full rates, and Permian production remained above 1 million BOE/d. These factors, combined with stronger oil and gas prices, could have lifted upstream earnings even after accounting for an estimated 100,000-150,000 BOE per day turnaround impact. Consequently, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the second-quarter upstream segment is currently pegged at a profit of $8.3 billion compared to the year-ago income of $2.7 billion. Chevron's downstream business likely received support from improved refining margins and higher utilization across its global refining network. Management indicated that U.S. refineries achieved record crude throughput, while Asia refinery utilization was expected to remain around 80% during the second quarter. The company also emphasized growing integration benefits by directing more equity crude into its refining system, helping capture additional value across the supply chain. Historical trends further suggest that downstream earnings have frequently exceeded expectations, with the segment posting positive earnings surprises in several recent quarters, including 36.5% in first-quarter 2026 and 16.7% in second-quarter 2025. According to the Zacks Consensus Estimate, downstream income is expected to jump to some $4 billion from just $737 million in second-quarter 2025. But on a somewhat bearish note, Chevron's second-quarter earnings could have faced pressure from elevated investment spending alongside softer downstream sales volumes. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for second-quarter 2026 capital expenditures is pegged at about $4.7 billion, well above the $3.7 billion reported in the year-ago quarter. At the same time, consensus mark for worldwide refined product sales of roughly 2.7 million barrels per day is slightly below the second-quarter 2025 levels. Rival ExxonMobil HoldingsXOM heads into its second-quarter earnings with stronger oil prices expected to have been the biggest driver of results. ExxonMobil estimates that higher liquids prices alone could have lifted earnings by about $3.5-$3.9 billion from the prior quarter. ExxonMobil also expects better refining, chemicals and specialty product margins to have provided an additional boost. These positives are likely to have outweighed production disruptions linked to the Middle East conflict, although management has cautioned that operational shutdowns and supply interruptions will have partly offset the benefits. Meanwhile, European oil major Shell plcSHEL has outlined a mixed but improving outlook. Shell expects lower gas production because of disruptions in Qatar linked to the Middle East conflict, but stronger gas trading should help offset much of that weakness. Shell is also benefiting from improved refining and chemicals margins, refinery utilization near full capacity and a recovery in working capital, all of which should support cash flow. While geopolitical risks remain, the company's diversified operations provide several earnings drivers beyond production volumes. Shares of Chevron have gone up 11% in the past six-month period compared with the broader Zacks Energy sector’s growth of 11.7%. Shares of XOM have gained 10.1%, while SHEL stock has gone up 11.5%. From a valuation perspective — in terms of forward price-to-earnings ratio — Chevron is trading at a premium compared to the industry average. The stock is also trading above its five-year mean of 11.81. Chevron enters its second-quarter earnings release with solid operating momentum and a generally balanced outlook. Higher production from the Permian Basin, Tengiz and LNG assets, together with stronger commodity prices and improved refining margins, should support a substantial year-over-year earnings increase. The company’s cost-reduction initiatives and consistent shareholder distributions further strengthen its investment case. The Microsoft power agreement also creates a potential long-term growth avenue tied to rising data-center electricity demand. However, elevated capital spending and slightly weaker refined-product sales volumes could limit near-term upside. Overall, Chevron’s strengths and risks appear evenly balanced ahead of the results. The oil and gas sector underpins the global economy, supplying the energy that powers transportation, industry, and everyday life. It stretches across a long chain of activity, from exploring for and producing crude and natural gas, through refining raw hydrocarbons into usable fuels, to marketing those products to customers around the world. Prices along this chain are set in global markets that respond to the balance of supply and demand, a balance that can shift quickly in response to economic conditions, production decisions, and geopolitical events. Because energy is so essential and so widely traded, the sector reacts sharply to headlines, and a single development in a distant region can move prices everywhere. That sensitivity was on display over the weekend as an easing of tensions sent crude lower and pressured the shares of the largest producers. Chevron is an integrated major, operating across the full length of the oil and gas chain rather than concentrating on any single segment. Its upstream business explores for and produces crude and natural gas from fields around the world, anchored by a substantial position in the prolific basins of the American Southwest. Its downstream operations refine crude into fuels and lubricants and market those products to customers. And its chemicals arm turns hydrocarbons into the building blocks of countless everyday products. The company is also pursuing lower-carbon efforts in areas such as renewable fuels, hydrogen, and carbon capture. This breadth is the essence of the integrated model, giving the company a measure of balance across the cycle, since weakness in one part of the chain can sometimes be offset by strength in another. This is why the movements of crude and the reporting from the major producers draw such close attention, offering a read on the global economy that reaches far beyond the oil and gas sector itself.                                        My Trusted Source Chevron (NYSE:CVX) is heading into its next round of quarterly results with domestic production having topped two million oil-equivalent barrels per day across consecutive quarters, a milestone that has drawn attention to the strength of the company's onshore and offshore portfolio within the United States. The figure, sustained over more than a single reporting period, marks a notable point in the company's long-running effort to grow its domestic footprint while maintaining the integrated upstream-and-downstream structure that has defined its business model for decades. Reaching and sustaining domestic output above two million oil-equivalent barrels per day did not happen overnight. Chevron has spent years building out its position in the Permian Basin, one of the most prolific unconventional resource plays in the world, while also advancing offshore projects in the Gulf of Mexico that contribute meaningful volumes of both oil and natural gas. The combination of onshore unconventional drilling and offshore deepwater production gives the company a domestic base that is unusually diversified relative to many peers that lean more heavily on a single basin or asset type. The Permian Basin, spanning parts of West Texas and southeastern New Mexico, has been central to this growth. Chevron has continued to apply longer lateral wells, tighter well spacing where geology allows, and data-driven completion designs aimed at extracting more barrels per well while containing costs. These efficiency gains have become increasingly important as the basin matures and the easiest, highest-quality drilling locations become scarcer, requiring operators to work harder to sustain output growth from what remains. Alongside the Permian, Chevron's offshore Gulf of Mexico assets continue to contribute a steady stream of production from deepwater fields that benefit from lower per-barrel operating costs once initial development capital has been deployed. These offshore assets tend to produce with less volatility than unconventional wells, which typically show steep initial output followed by a rapid decline, meaning the Gulf of Mexico portfolio provides a stabilizing complement to the faster-cycle Permian program. Chevron has continued to advance select offshore projects aimed at tying back new subsea wells to existing production platforms, a lower-cost approach to growing offshore output compared with sanctioning entirely new standalone developments. The combination of these two domestic engines, one onshore and fast-cycle, the other offshore and long-cycle, has allowed Chevron to sustain the elevated output levels now being highlighted heading into its next results. Sustaining this level across consecutive quarters, rather than achieving it as a single high-water mark, is itself a meaningful signal about the durability of the underlying production base rather than a one-time event driven by a handful of new wells coming online simultaneously. Chevron's integrated structure, spanning upstream exploration and production alongside downstream refining and marketing operations, remains a defining feature of how the company is evaluated heading into quarterly results. The upstream segment tends to benefit when crude prices firm, as has been the case recently amid supply management from major producing nations and disruptions affecting shipping routes used by crude and liquefied-gas carriers. The downstream segment, by contrast, often performs best when refining margins widen, a dynamic that can move independently of, and at times inversely to, crude price trends. This structural balance means that Chevron's overall results depend on the interplay between these two segments rather than on either one in isolation. When crude prices rise sharply, downstream margins can compress if refined product prices fail to keep pace, while a period of softer crude prices can sometimes coincide with wider refining margins as input costs ease faster than product prices adjust. Market participants heading into the upcoming results will likely weigh how this balance played out across the reporting period, alongside the headline domestic production figures. The broader crude price environment heading into Chevron's results has been shaped by a mix of factors, including production decisions from major exporting nations, resilient demand from large industrial economies, and periodic disruptions to shipping lanes used by tankers carrying crude oil and liquefied natural gas. These disruptions have, at various points, added a premium to crude pricing as market participants account for the added cost, delay, and insurance complexity associated with rerouting cargoes around affected corridors. For a company with Chevron's scale of domestic and international upstream exposure, this backdrop has generally been supportive of upstream price realizations, even as downstream margins face their own separate set of pressures tied to seasonal product demand patterns and refining capacity utilization across the industry. The net effect of these crosscurrents will be one of the central storylines market watchers focus on when the company reports. Chevron competes within a field of large integrated energy companies that includes ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), which has similarly emphasized capital discipline and portfolio concentration around its highest-return basins, including its own substantial Permian position and offshore developments in Guyana. Both companies have pursued broadly similar strategies in recent years, favoring measured production growth funded largely through operating cash flow rather than aggressive expansion financed through additional borrowing. Beyond the largest integrated majors, Chevron also faces competition from independent exploration and production companies concentrated in the Permian and other domestic basins, as well as from companies with more specialized positions such as Cheniere Energy (NYSE:LNG) in the liquefied natural gas export space. While Cheniere's business model differs meaningfully from Chevron's integrated structure, both companies benefit from many of the same underlying demand trends tied to natural gas, whether that demand manifests as export volumes or as feedstock for domestic power generation and industrial use. Chevron has continued to emphasize a capital allocation framework that prioritizes projects capable of generating steady cash flow at a range of crude price levels, rather than pursuing volume growth as an end in itself. This discipline has shaped decisions across the portfolio, from the pace of drilling activity in the Permian to the sequencing of offshore project sanctions in the Gulf of Mexico and in international basins. The approach reflects a broader shift across the integrated energy sector, where companies have generally moved toward prioritizing free cash flow generation and steady capital allocation over the volume-growth-focused strategies that characterized earlier industry cycles. This capital discipline also extends to how Chevron approaches its international portfolio, which includes positions in the Eastern Mediterranean, West Africa, and other regions that contribute production and cash flow alongside the domestic base. Balancing capital across this global footprint while sustaining the domestic output levels now being highlighted requires continuous prioritization decisions, particularly in a period when many companies across the sector are simultaneously competing for drilling equipment, skilled labor, and midstream capacity in the most active basins. Natural gas has taken on growing strategic importance across the energy sector, both as a power-generation fuel supporting rising electricity demand and as an export commodity moving through liquefied natural gas terminals along the Gulf Coast. Chevron's own natural gas production, both domestic and international, positions it to benefit from these broader trends, even though its commercial exposure to liquefied natural gas exports is more limited than that of dedicated exporters. The company's natural gas volumes nonetheless contribute meaningfully to its overall oil-equivalent production figures, including the domestic output levels now being highlighted heading into results. The broader shift toward natural gas as a bridge fuel, supporting power generation for data centers and industrial electrification while lower-carbon technologies continue to scale, has reinforced the strategic value of companies with substantial gas positions. This dynamic touches companies across the Energy Stocks category, from integrated majors like Chevron to renewable-focused companies such as NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE), which has increasingly leaned on gas-fired generation alongside its renewable portfolio to meet rising electricity demand. Chevron has maintained a long-standing commitment to consistent stockholder distributions through dividends and buyback programs, a practice the company has continued through periods of commodity price volatility. Heading into its next results, market participants will likely pay close attention to how the company balances continued distributions against capital spending commitments tied to sustaining the elevated domestic production levels and advancing international projects. This balance has become an increasingly central theme in how integrated energy companies communicate capital allocation priorities, particularly as sustained higher domestic output requires ongoing reinvestment to offset natural decline rates in unconventional wells. The company's approach in this regard mirrors broader industry trends, with peers similarly emphasizing steady distributions funded by disciplined capital spending rather than volume growth pursued without regard to capital efficiency. As Chevron approaches its results, the durability of the domestic output milestone, alongside the performance of the downstream segment and the broader crude price backdrop, together with shipping-related disruptions affecting global energy flows, will likely shape how the results are received. The interplay between these upstream and downstream dynamics, set against the backdrop of the broader S&P 500, continues to make Chevron a closely watched name within the integrated energy space. Sustaining production at these levels requires continuous spending on personnel, equipment, and midstream infrastructure capable of moving barrels from the wellhead to market. Chevron has continued to expand its workforce and contractor base across its most active domestic basins, competing for skilled labor alongside other operators in a tight regional labor market. Midstream capacity, including pipelines and processing facilities needed to handle both oil and associated natural gas volumes, has also required ongoing coordination with third-party infrastructure providers to avoid bottlenecks that could otherwise constrain output growth. These operational considerations, while less visible than headline production figures, remain central to whether the company can sustain its current output trajectory across coming reporting periods. The consecutive-quarter nature of the current milestone indicates these underlying operational elements have been functioning smoothly, though continued execution will remain necessary to maintain the pace achieved thus far. Chevron's downstream operations span a network of refineries and marketing operations that convert crude oil into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other refined products distributed across domestic and international markets. Refining margins have moved through a choppy pattern this year, shaped by seasonal driving demand, jet fuel consumption tied to air travel activity, and periodic maintenance turnarounds that temporarily reduce processing capacity across the industry. These turnarounds, while planned well in advance, can create short-term tightness in regional product markets, occasionally widening margins for refiners with available capacity to step in and meet demand. The chemical and lubricants businesses nested within Chevron's downstream segment add a further layer of diversification, supplying feedstocks and finished products used across packaging, construction, and industrial applications. These businesses tend to move on a somewhat different cycle than fuel refining, tied more closely to broader industrial production trends than to seasonal transportation demand, giving Chevron another source of balance within its overall downstream contribution. When measured against ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), Chevron presents a somewhat more concentrated domestic production base, with a larger proportional share of total output coming from United States basins relative to its larger peer, which maintains a more globally distributed upstream portfolio anchored by its Guyana development alongside its own substantial Permian position. This difference in geographic concentration shapes how each company's results respond to domestic versus international price and regulatory dynamics, even though both companies pursue broadly similar capital discipline principles. Chevron's international portfolio, while smaller as a share of the total than its domestic base, still contributes meaningfully to overall results, spanning positions in the Eastern Mediterranean, West Africa, and other regions. Balancing capital across this global footprint while simultaneously sustaining the domestic output levels now being highlighted requires ongoing prioritization, particularly during periods when multiple regions compete for the same pool of available capital and technical resources. The broader upstream sector has continued to navigate a period in which demand for drilling rigs, hydraulic fracturing equipment, and skilled field personnel remains elevated across the most active domestic basins. Chevron, like its peers, has had to manage service cost inflation tied to this demand, working with oilfield service providers to secure equipment availability and pricing that supports continued drilling activity without eroding the capital efficiency gains achieved through technology and design improvements in recent years. Labor availability has similarly remained a point of ongoing management attention, with companies across the sector competing for engineers, geoscientists, and field technicians capable of supporting both the fast-cycle unconventional drilling programs and the more specialized offshore development work that together make up Chevron's domestic production base. These workforce dynamics, while less visible in headline reporting, underpin the operational execution needed to sustain output at the levels the company has now maintained across consecutive quarters. Chevron's position within the broader energy sector reflects a company balancing steady domestic growth against a global portfolio and an integrated structure that spans the full value chain from wellhead to refined product. This positioning differs from more narrowly focused companies such as Cheniere Energy (NYSE:LNG), which concentrates almost entirely on liquefied natural gas export infrastructure, or from renewable-focused companies such as NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE), which has built its business around wind, solar, and battery storage alongside a regulated utility operation. The diversity of business models across these companies illustrates the breadth of the modern energy sector, which now spans traditional integrated oil and gas production, dedicated natural gas export infrastructure, and renewable power generation, all coexisting and, in some respects, increasingly intertwined as natural gas serves as a bridge fuel supporting the broader shift toward lower-carbon power generation. Chevron's upcoming results will offer a window into how the traditional integrated model is performing amid these broader sector currents, with the sustained domestic production milestone serving as one of several data points market participants will weigh alongside downstream margins and capital spending trends. The move, announced as part of the company's routine dividend update, continues a pattern that has held through multiple commodity cycles, including periods of sharply falling crude prices, swinging refining margins, and broader macroeconomic turbulence. Energy companies operate in one of the more cyclical corners of the market, with crude and natural gas benchmarks swinging widely based on global supply decisions, geopolitical tension, and demand shifts tied to industrial activity and travel patterns. Against that backdrop, maintaining a multi-decade streak of annual dividend increases is a notable feat, one that requires disciplined spending, a diversified asset base, and a willingness to prioritize steady payout growth over aggressive expansion during periods of elevated commodity pricing. Chevron's approach has generally leaned on balancing upstream production growth with downstream refining and chemical operations, giving it multiple sources of earnings that do not always move in lockstep. When crude prices soften, refining margins can sometimes widen as input costs fall faster than product prices adjust, providing a partial offset. This diversified structure has been part of why Chevron has been able to keep raising its payout even during years when energy benchmarks were under considerable pressure. Chevron's asset base spans exploration and production across several continents, with meaningful positions in shale formations domestically as well as deepwater and international projects. The company also operates a network of refineries and chemical facilities that convert crude and natural gas into fuels, lubricants, and petrochemical building blocks used across manufacturing and transportation. Recent operational emphasis has centered on squeezing more efficiency from existing production rather than chasing large new projects, a trend that has become common across the energy sector since the last major downturn reshaped spending habits industry-wide. Chevron has also continued to integrate assets gained through a large-scale combination completed in recent years, aiming to extract efficiencies across overlapping operations while streamlining its overall production base. Natural gas remains another pillar of the business, with liquefied natural gas projects and domestic gas production contributing to overall output. As global demand for cleaner-burning fuels continues to evolve, natural gas has occupied a middle ground between traditional crude-heavy portfolios and newer low-carbon energy sources, and Chevron has positioned parts of its asset base to capture that demand. The broader energy sector has been navigating a period of transition, with traditional producers balancing near-term demand for oil and gas against longer-term questions about the pace of the shift toward renewable and lower-carbon energy stock sources. Regulatory frameworks in various regions continue to evolve, shaping everything from emissions reporting requirements to incentives tied to carbon capture and alternative fuels. At the same time, global supply dynamics tied to coordinated production decisions among major exporting nations continue to influence pricing. Periods of coordinated supply restraint have at times supported crude benchmarks, while other stretches have seen elevated output pressure pricing lower. This push and pull has kept energy earnings inherently variable even as demand for transportation fuels and petrochemical feedstocks has remained broadly resilient. Energy stocks broadly have moved through a stretch marked by choppy trading, with crude benchmarks fluctuating on a mix of supply headlines, demand data out of major economies, and currency movements. Refining margins have also swung, at times compressing as product inventories built up and at other times widening when seasonal demand for fuels picked up. Against this backdrop, market participants have paid close attention to how energy majors balance capital spending on new projects against cash channeled to those who own their shares. Chevron's continued willingness to raise its payout even through uneven commodity pricing has been viewed by some market watchers as a signal of confidence in the durability of its free cash generation across a range of pricing environments. Dividend growth among large energy companies has followed varied paths in recent years. Some producers pulled back or paused payout growth during the depths of past downturns, only to resume increases once cash flows stabilized. Chevron stands out for having avoided such a pause, maintaining its streak of annual increases even through the most severe commodity slump in recent memory. That consistency has helped Chevron build a track record that places it among a relatively small group of companies across all sectors, not just energy, with multi-decade streaks of annual dividend growth. Within the category of dividend stocks, energy names with such long streaks are comparatively rare given the sector's inherent cyclicality, which makes Chevron's record a point of distinction among market watchers who track long-term payout growth. Chevron's continued streak also places it in the conversation alongside other long-tenured dividend growers across sectors, from consumer staples names to industrial companies that have similarly prioritized steady payout growth through economic cycles. Within the energy sector specifically, few companies can point to as long an unbroken run of annual increases, giving Chevron a distinct position among its direct peers. That position has been reinforced by the company's continued membership among widely followed benchmark constituents, including the S&P 500, where it stands as one of the primary energy representatives alongside a small number of other sector names. The size and timing of the latest increase reflect a continuation of the gradual, measured approach Chevron has generally taken to payout growth, favoring steady, sustainable increases over sharp jumps tied to any single strong earnings period. This measured cadence has helped the company avoid the kind of dividend cuts that have occasionally hit energy peers during sharp downturns, since a more conservative growth rate leaves additional room to maintain payments even when cash flow softens temporarily. Market commentary following the announcement has generally framed the move as consistent with expectations, given the company's public commitment to maintaining its streak and its historical pattern of announcing increases around the same point in its fiscal calendar. The increase also arrives alongside continued capital discipline on the spending side, with the company continuing to prioritize projects that can generate solid economics across a range of commodity price scenarios rather than pursuing volume growth for its own sake. Chevron has continued to emphasize a handful of operational priorities, including maximizing output from its most productive shale acreage, advancing select deepwater projects with strong economics, and growing its natural gas and liquefied natural gas positions to serve both domestic and international demand. The company has also continued to fund selective lower-carbon initiatives, including carbon capture, hydrogen, and renewable fuel projects, though these remain a smaller part of the overall portfolio relative to traditional oil and gas operations. Cost discipline has remained a consistent theme, with the company continuing to look for efficiency gains across its combined asset base following its recent large-scale combination. Integration efforts have focused on eliminating overlapping functions, streamlining supply chains, and applying best practices across newly combined operations to support steady free cash generation over time. Several headwinds continue to face energy producers broadly. Demand growth for traditional transportation fuels faces gradual pressure from the slow but steady adoption of electric vehicles in some markets, even as demand in other regions continues to grow. Regulatory pressure tied to emissions reduction goals continues to add compliance costs and complexity, particularly in regions with aggressive climate rules. Geopolitical tension in key producing regions also remains a persistent factor that can disrupt supply chains or add volatility to pricing with little advance warning. Currency fluctuations, particularly moves in the dollar relative to other major currencies, can also influence the relative cost of crude for nations that import it, adding another layer of variability to global demand patterns. Compared with domestic peers such as Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM), Chevron has generally maintained a somewhat smaller overall production base but has been recognized for similarly disciplined capital allocation. ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP), which operates a more purely upstream-focused business without significant downstream refining, offers a useful point of contrast, since its earnings tend to track crude and gas prices more directly without the partial offset that refining margins can provide. Chevron's streak of annual dividend increases traces back through a long stretch of energy sector history, including the sharp downturn triggered by a historic collapse in global oil demand, several periods of oversupply driven by rapid growth in shale output, and multiple episodes of coordinated production cuts among major exporting nations aimed at stabilizing prices. Through each of these episodes, the company continued to raise its payout, even in years when overall earnings came under considerable pressure. That resilience has often been attributed to a conservative approach to balance-sheet management, including a willingness to take on additional debt temporarily during severe downturns rather than cut the payout, paired with a commitment to reduce that debt again once conditions normalized. This willingness to smooth results across the cycle, rather than mirror the full swings of commodity pricing in the payout itself, has been a defining feature of Chevron's approach relative to some peers that have been quicker to cut during difficult stretches. Looking across the years ahead, several structural themes are likely to continue shaping how energy majors including Chevron approach capital spending and payout growth. The pace at which global electricity generation and transportation shift toward lower-carbon sources will influence long-term demand assumptions for crude and natural gas, even as most projections continue to point to continued substantial demand for these fuels for an extended stretch of time. Meanwhile, capital discipline across the broader energy sector, a theme that took root industry-wide following the sharpest downturns of the past several cycles, appears likely to persist, with companies generally continuing to favor measured production growth and steady payout increases over the more aggressive expansion strategies that characterized earlier periods of the industry's history. Chevron's continued adherence to this disciplined approach will likely remain a point of reference for those studying how large energy companies navigate a changing demand landscape. For those following the category of dividend stocks, Chevron's continued streak of annual increases offers a data point on how a cyclical, capital-intensive business can still support steady payout growth through disciplined spending and a diversified asset base. The company's approach, which favors measured increases over aggressive jumps, has helped it avoid the boom-and-bust payout patterns that have characterized some other energy names during periods of sharp commodity swings. Broader macroeconomic conditions, including interest-rate trends and currency movements, will likely continue to shape how energy majors including Chevron balance capital spending, debt levels, and payout growth across the years ahead. Market watchers who track long-term dividend growers will likely continue to view Chevron's streak as a reference point within the broader energy sector. title: Pre-Markets Fill Holes Left from Friday's Selloff - The Globe and Mail
content: Monday, July 27th, 2026Pre-market futures are improving this morning, after closing out last week’s trading on weaker footing. The blue-chip Dow is presently up +580 points, +1.1% and the S&P 500 +60 points, +0.81%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq leads the way +357, +1.26%, while the small-cap Russell 2000 is +2 points at this hour, +0.06%. Tensions in and around Iran cooled over the weekend, bringing down spot oil prices as well.We also see the latest publicly traded memory chip company this morning: CXMT Corp., formerly ChangXin Memory Technology, is setting records as the newest entrant on the Shanghai STAR exchange. The Chinese AI play rose +466% in its first day of trading, making it the largest semiconductor company in the history of the Shanghai market. Compare this with South Korea’s SK Hynix SKHY, which is up +3.8% today, and Micron TechnologiesMU, +1% in today’s pre-market. Headline Durable Goods Orders for June came in a small fraction of expectations: +0.3% from a consensus estimate of +2%. Technically, this is the third positive print in the last four months, and comes off the lowest month of the year: -4.5% in May. These are preliminary numbers that will smooth out in a couple weeks, but its clear durable goods orders are seeking equilibrium.Ex-Transportation, its +0.6% reached only a third of the prior month’s upwardly revised +1.8%. Non-Defense, ex-aircraft (a proxy for normal enterprise spending) came in at +0.9%, 20 basis points (bps) higher than projections, and rose half a point on the May revision to +1.9%. Shipments roared ahead +1.9% — the highest tally we’ve seen since 2021. Q2 earnings season shifts to a higher gear this week, with “Mag 7” stocks Meta PlatformsMETA and MicrosoftMSFT releasing quarterly results Wednesday after the close. AppleAAPL and AmazonAMZN report on Thursday afternoon — and Apple should be interesting, as it has begged off the AI race and thus will not see a considerable hit to free cash flow. Will this make a difference to investors?Besides these important earnings reports, we’ll see Q2 results for BoeingBA Tuesday morning, with Exxon Mobil XOM and ChevronCVX Friday ahead of the bell. These are but a smidgeon of the more than 900 companies scheduled to report quarterly earnings this week alone. Commencing tomorrow and concluding Wednesday afternoon, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on monetary policy this week. Odds are strong that the 3.50-3.75% Fed funds rate will remain in place, where it has been all year. Biases had been for a downward move on the Fed’s next policy shift, but in recent months with the Iran war ongoing, high oil prices (Brent crude rose above $100 per barrel last week) are turning the tide in FOMC sentiment toward a rate hike sometime this year.Questions or comments about this article and/or author? Space is projected to become a trillion dollar industry, and this company's customer base is growing fast. Analysts have forecasted a major revenue breakout in 2025. Chevron Corporation CVX has strengthened its offshore Malaysia development plans after its subsidiary, Hess Exploration and Production Malaysia, awarded Velesto Drilling a $51 million contract for integrated rig, drilling and completion (i-RDC) services, according to Offshore Magazine. The contract supports the 2026-2028 North Malay Basin Full Field Development campaign, reinforcing ongoing efforts to sustain gas production from one of Malaysia's key offshore energy hubs. The award marks another important milestone in the long-standing collaboration between the companies and further expands Velesto Drilling's role in the North Malay Basin development program. As part of the agreement, the NAGA 8 jackup rig will be deployed for the campaign after completing its current assignment in Malaysia. Hess Exploration and Production Malaysia, now a Chevron subsidiary following its acquisition of Hess, continues to operate several gas-producing assets offshore Malaysia. The latest contract highlights Chevron's commitment to advancing the development of the North Malay Basin while maintaining operational continuity across its offshore portfolio. The North Malay Basin remains one of Malaysia's most significant offshore gas-producing regions, supplying natural gas for domestic industries as well as regional energy markets. Development activities in the basin have progressed through multiple drilling phases designed to sustain production and maximize recovery from existing producing fields. By awarding this integrated drilling contract, Chevron continues to support long-term field development while streamlining offshore operations through an integrated service model. The latest award represents Velesto Drilling's second i-RDC contract for the North Malay Basin Full Field Development. Under the i-RDC framework, the contractor delivers a bundled package that combines drilling rig services, drilling operations and well-completion services under a single contract. This integrated approach is intended to improve operational efficiency while reducing project interfaces between multiple service providers. The contract further strengthens Velesto's position within Malaysia's offshore drilling sector and reflects continued participation in Chevron-operated development campaigns across the North Malay Basin. According to the news, to execute the newly awarded project, Velesto Drilling will allocate the NAGA 8 jackup rig for operations associated with the North Malay Basin campaign. The drilling program is scheduled to begin next month, allowing the rig to transition directly from its current assignment. NAGA 8 is presently completing drilling activities for Jadestone Energy (Malaysia) under the East Belumut Phase 9 infill drilling project. Following completion of the existing work scope, the rig will move into the Chevron-operated campaign, supporting drilling and completion activities through the planned 2026-2028 development period. The deployment ensures continuity for the rig while supporting Chevron's long-term offshore development objectives in Malaysia. The North Malay Basin gas fields, located offshore Peninsular Malaysia, form an important component of Malaysia's offshore natural gas production network. The region has undergone phased field development programs focused on maintaining production from mature assets while maximizing hydrocarbon recovery. These drilling campaigns continue to play an important role in supporting reliable gas supplies for domestic industrial demand and regional energy markets. As development progresses, integrated drilling campaigns remain central to improving operational coordination and execution across multiple offshore wells. The latest contract reinforces continued activity within one of Malaysia's most active offshore drilling regions while supporting future field development objectives. The i-RDC structure adopted for the North Malay Basin campaign combines several critical offshore services into a unified operational framework. Rather than managing separate drilling, rig and completion contracts, the integrated model enables a single contractor to coordinate multiple project components. This approach is intended to improve workflow efficiency, reduce operational interfaces and simplify project execution throughout the drilling campaign. For long-term offshore developments involving multiple wells, integrated contracting models can provide greater operational consistency across different phases of field development. The North Malay Basin campaign continues this approach, building upon previous integrated drilling programs in the region. The new contract further extends Velesto Drilling's footprint within Malaysia's offshore energy sector. Its continued involvement in the North Malay Basin demonstrates the company's established role in supporting offshore gas development programs operated by Chevron. Securing a second i-RDC award for the basin also reflects the continuation of an existing working relationship on one of Malaysia's most active offshore development projects. The multi-year nature of the campaign positions the company for sustained operational activity while supporting ongoing offshore drilling efforts in the region. Before receiving the North Malay Basin award, Velesto Drilling and PETRONAS North Ketapang agreed earlier this week to terminate a contract involving the NAGA 8 jackup rig for offshore Indonesia. With the Malaysian development campaign scheduled to begin next month, the rig will transition from its current Malaysia assignment into the Chevron-operated North Malay Basin program. The new deployment ensures that NAGA 8 remains engaged in offshore drilling operations while supporting continued field development activities in Malaysia. The integrated drilling and completion contract awarded by a Chevron subsidiary reinforces the ongoing development of the North Malay Basin Full Field Development campaign. By selecting Velesto Drilling and deploying the NAGA 8 jackup rig, Chevron continues advancing offshore gas development in Malaysia through an integrated operational model designed to support drilling efficiency and sustained production from one of the country's key offshore gas regions. This integrated structure allows the company to participate across several stages of the energy value chain rather than relying on a single business activity. Higher crude prices can support upstream earnings because the company receives stronger returns from produced oil and natural gas. The central issue is whether stronger commodity conditions can translate into durable financial improvement rather than temporary earnings support. Chevrons production growth remains an important part of its long-term business narrative. The company has expanded output from major operations, including assets in the Permian Basin and projects connected with its broader portfolio expansion. The Permian Basin is one of North Americas most productive oil and natural gas regions. Chevrons scale in the area provides access to established infrastructure, extensive drilling inventory, and operational efficiencies that may support dependable production. Additional assets in Guyana and the Bakken region broaden the companys geographic exposure. Guyana has emerged as an important offshore production center, while the Bakken remains a significant North American shale region. This diversified production base can support revenue stability, particularly when individual projects experience operational challenges. It also helps Chevron respond to rising global energy demand across developing economies and established industrial markets. Chevrons expanded asset portfolio may strengthen its ability to generate cash across different market environments. Large acquisitions can create access to new production regions, specialized expertise, and longer-duration development opportunities. The strategic value of these assets depends on successful integration. Chevron must coordinate operating systems, capital allocation, project development, and cost controls across a larger organization. Effective integration could support stronger margins and broader production growth. Weak execution, however, could increase expenses or delay the financial benefits expected from the enlarged portfolio. The companys ability to convert additional resources into reliable output will therefore remain a major factor shaping its longer-term valuation. Chevron has maintained a long record of regular shareholder distributions, reflecting managements focus on disciplined capital allocation and dependable cash generation. Energy earnings can fluctuate with crude prices, refining margins, operating costs, and economic conditions. Maintaining distributions through changing market cycles requires balance-sheet flexibility and careful spending decisions. Chevrons established distribution history may signal confidence in the durability of its operations. However, future payments still depend on cash flow, capital requirements, project spending, and commodity conditions. The company must balance shareholder returns with investment in exploration, production, infrastructure, and lower-carbon initiatives. Excessive spending could weaken financial flexibility, while insufficient investment could limit future production capacity. Chevrons valuation presents a more complicated picture than its recent momentum alone might suggest. Some intrinsic valuation approaches indicate that the companys expected revenue growth, production expansion, and future margins could support a higher long-term valuation. These frameworks emphasize future cash generation and the value of assets expected to contribute over many years. Earnings-based measures present a more cautious interpretation. Global population growth, industrial development, transportation needs, and expanding electricity consumption continue supporting demand for reliable energy supplies. Its broad operating reach provides exposure to both traditional energy demand and evolving market requirements. Long-term uncertainty remains important. Faster adoption of alternative energy sources, regulatory changes, carbon reduction policies, and improved efficiency could gradually affect oil demand. Chevron must therefore manage current production opportunities while adapting its portfolio for a changing global energy system. The companys ability to invest carefully without weakening returns will influence its competitive position. These strengths provide a credible foundation for continued business performance. However, the current valuation leaves limited room for major operational setbacks. Large projects must remain on schedule, integration efforts must deliver expected benefits, and production growth must translate into dependable cash flow. Middle East tensions may support near-term energy pricing, but the companys lasting valuation case rests on factors it can control: operational efficiency, disciplined spending, project delivery, and portfolio management. Chevrons next phase will be defined not simply by crude prices, but by whether its expanding operations can generate sustainable value through changing market conditions. title: U.S. Farmers Spent $1.4 Billion More On Diesel This Spring - The Globe and Mail
content: Rising fuel costs led American farmers to spend $1.4 billion U.S. more on diesel during the spring planting season this year. A study by the Joint Economic Committee found farmers in the U.S. spent considerably more on diesel fuel than they did last season as energy costs spiked due to the Iran war. The study looked at the cost inputs involved in planting key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat, and rice among U.S. farmers. The increase in diesel spending to plant those crops represented a 63% year-over-year jump, according to the analysis. Calculations were made using data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) and estimates of average fuel use by crop supplied by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The study found that farmers in Illinois, Iowa, and Minnesota saw the highest increase in diesel costs this spring when crude oil prices topped $110 U.S. a barrel. The analysis found that the price to refill a farm's onsite fuel tank increased an average of $1,538 U.S. across 49 of America's 50 states. The U.S. farm lobby has been calling for more economic relief from the administration of President Donald Trump, arguing that rising fuel costs are hurting their margins and profits. title: Energy Stocks Tumble After Oil Suffers Biggest Drop in Months - TradingView
content: Oil prices retreated sharply Monday, pulling energy shares lower after the United States and Iran paused military strikes over the weekend, easing immediate concerns about disruptions to global crude supplies. Energy producers and refiners moved lower in premarket trading alongside the drop in crude. BP (BP) lost about 3.5%, Exxon Mobil XXOM declined 3%, Chevron CVX slipped 3%, and Shell SHEL eased 1.8%. Among exploration companies, Diamondback Energy (FANG) fell 3.8%, while Devon Energy (DVN), Occidental Petroleum (OXY) and ConocoPhillips (COP) each traded lower. West Texas Intermediate crude fell about 8.8% to $82.48 a barrel, while Brent crude dropped roughly 10% to $87.93. The decline followed signs of reduced tensions, although shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has yet to recover as markets await greater clarity on whether the pause will hold. Refining stocks also weakened, with Valero Energy VLO and Marathon Petroleum (MPC) down about 3% and Phillips 66 (PSX) off 2.8%. Market participants continue monitoring diplomatic efforts and vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz for signs that crude exports could normalize. Chevron Corporation is an American multinational energy firm primarily focused on oil and gas. As the second-largest direct descendant of Standard Oil, originally known as the Standard Oil Company of California, it operates in more than 180 countries. Chevron is vertically integrated within the oil and gas sector, engaging in hydrocarbon exploration, production, refining, marketing and transportation, chemical manufacturing and sales, as well as power generation. Originally founded in Southern California in the 1870s, the company was based in San Francisco, California, for many years before relocating its corporate headquarters to San Ramon, California, in 2001. As of August 2, 2024, Chevron announced plans to shift its headquarters from California to Houston, Texas. The company’s history can be traced back to the latter part of the 19th century, when it was formed from small California oil companies that were acquired by Standard Oil and merged into Standard Oil of California. Following the breakup of Standard Oil, Chevron rapidly expanded by continuing to acquire and partner with other firms both within and outside California, ultimately becoming one of the Seven Sisters, which dominated the global oil industry from the mid-1940s to the 1970s. In 1985, the company, then known as Socal, merged with Gulf Oil, headquartered in Pittsburgh, and rebranded as Chevron. This merged entity later joined forces with Texaco in 2001. Chevron manufactures and markets fuels, lubricants, additives, and petrochemicals, primarily in Western North America, the US Gulf Coast, Southeast Asia, South Korea, and Australia. In 2018, Chevron produced an average of 791,000 barrels of net oil-equivalent per day in the United States. As one of the largest companies globally, Chevron is the second-largest oil firm based in the United States by revenue, trailing only fellow Standard Oil descendant ExxonMobil. In 2024, Chevron ranked 16th on the Fortune 500. Additionally, it remains the sole oil-and-gas component of the Dow Jones Industrial Average following ExxonMobil's exit from the index in 2020.

content: Shares of Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and Chevron Corp. (CVX) were mixed in early premarket trading on Friday as oil prices soared over $100 a barrel on Thursday. XOM stock is up nearly 28% so far in 2026 and CVX stock has gained about 25% in the same time. Yet, Piper Sandler sees further upside in both stocks. Piper Sandler assumed coverage of Exxon Mobil on Thursday with a ‘Neutral’ rating and $158 price target, implying an upside of nearly 1%, as per TheFly. The company's "low" balance sheet makes room for steady capital allocation execution through the market cycle, the analyst reportedly said, but added that it believes Exxon is trading near fair value multiples on 2027 estimates. Meanwhile, Piper Sandler assumed coverage of Chevron with an ‘Overweight’ rating and $207 price target, implying an upside of about 6.5% from its last close. The analyst said the company has removed two key valuation overhangs over the past year: uncertainty surrounding the completion of the Hess acquisition and the successful startup of the Tengiz Future Growth Project (TCO FGP). The firm also noted that the company is entering a period of stronger organic cash flow growth as capital spending, excluding the Hess acquisition, continues to decline. Oil prices have been climbing amid the standoff between the U.S. and Iran as American forces attacked the Middle Eastern country for a 13th consecutive night on Thursday. Brent crude prices rose to over $100 a barrel before declining to about $98.90 at the time of writing. WTI crude was trading around $90.57. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around XOM and CVX stocks was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing amid ‘normal’ message volumes. Both tickers were trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Meanwhile, the State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) was trading lower at the time of writing amid ‘bullish’ sentiment. One user said, “$XLE $XOM $CVX $OXY These should all be up more than 4% today on this immense move up to $100 bbl drizzy.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Intel Corp.’s stock rose nearly 4% in early premarket trading on Friday after the chipmaker’s upbeat quarterly results outweighed pressure from a broad selloff in South Korean chip stocks. Intel’s shares had climbed as high as 12% in Thursday’s after-market session just after the report. South Korea’s KOSPI declined 5.8% by Friday afternoon in Seoul, while Samsung and SK Hynix stocks slid 7.6% and 8.3%. The move in U.S. semiconductor stocks has become increasingly bundled with KOSPI, which is heavily weighted toward chipmakers Samsung and SK Hynix and has seen increased volatility lately. The Direxion Daily South Korea Bull 3X Shares (KORU), a three-times leveraged ETF tracking South Korea’s largest stocks, dropped 8.5%. The sentiment for the fund has dipped steadily over the past week and was ‘bearish’ as of the last reading. INTC was the top trending stock on Stocktwits early Friday, with retail sentiment moving to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘neutral’ the previous day. Retail traders debated the company’s capital expenditure plans and foundry business update, while analysts noted that Wall Street had largely expected a strong quarter, with much of the optimism already priced into the stock ahead of the earnings release. “INTC no way intel will stay at 100 and plus with that higher capex announcement wall street gonna dump on us,” a trader wrote, while another said, “$INTC can't hold a 9% gain for a few minutes, we're stuck here until 2027.” Intel plans to spend $20 billion this year, up from its previous forecast of $18 billion, and could tap the capital markets for funds. Tech giants Alphabet and Amazon recently raised enormous amounts through debt and equity despite having significant cash already. “INTC says they won't ramp Capex unless they were confident in customer commitments. Since they're raising Capex "significantly" next year, that means they're confident in those 10 long-term customers,” Deepwater Management founder Gene Munster said in an X post. Based on Intel’s fine print, Munster broadly believes that the AI infrastructure buildout is still in its early stages, with demand for its CPUs benefiting from the broader hyperscaler investment cycle. While he sees Intel as a beneficiary of the AI boom, he believes Nvidia and AMD remain better ways to invest in the trend, noting that much of Intel’s recent optimism is already reflected in its valuation. Intel’s turnaround is closely tied to its foundry business, which recently bagged new marquee customers such as Apple and Tesla. The unit narrowed its operating loss to $2.1 billion from a $3.2 billion loss a year earlier, but did not announce new customer wins in the report. The government-backed chipmaker’s second-quarter revenue increased 25% to $16.1 billion and adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.42 per share. Wall Street analysts had anticipated $14.5 billion in revenue and an adjusted profit of $0.22 per share, as per Fiscal.ai. The revenue expansion was largely driven by Intel’s data center operations, where sales soared 59% last quarter to $6.3 billion. "In data centers, the CPU is taking off," CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in an interview with Bloomberg. "Demand is outpacing our increasing supply, and so those are good problems to have." Intel’s third-quarter sales and profit forecasts also came in above expectations. As of the last close, INTC shares had declined 29% from their peak on June 22 but remain 172% higher year to date. (RTX) and Lockheed Martin (LMT) stocks are on track for weekly gains and have emerged as key beneficiaries of the renewed focus on defense spending after both companies delivered strong fiscal second-quarter (Q2) 2026 results and increased their outlooks for the year. RTX’s Q2 revenue and earnings grew at a double-digit pace across its three major businesses: Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney, and Raytheon. The company benefited from rising demand in both commercial aviation and defense markets, helping it deliver results that exceeded Wall Street expectations. RTX generated $2.9 billion in free cash flow during Q2, helped by $3.55 billion in operating cash flow. The company’s backlog surged to a record $289 billion, up 22% year-on-year, including $170 billion in commercial orders and $119 billion in defense contracts. RTX also added $43 billion in new bookings. The company raised its 2026 forecast, seeing revenue of $95 billion to $96 billion, compared with the prior estimate of $92.5 billion to $93.5 billion. RTX stock rose 0.3% overnight, ahead of Friday. The stock has gained 8% so far this week. “Raytheon booked nearly $20 billion of awards, resulting in a book-to-bill in Q2 of 2.4. These bookings included over $5 billion of GEM-T Patriot effectors driven by international customers and our first domestic GEM-T production order in over 30 years. Raytheon's bookings also included over $4 billion of classified and confidential awards as well as $1.8 billion for AMRAAM,” said RTX CEO Christopher Calio during the Q2 earnings call. Lockheed Martin posted a strong Q2 2026 performance, with higher revenue, improved profits, and $65 billion in new orders, helping the company recover from prior-year program losses and strengthening its future growth outlook. The company also generated $2.9 billion in free cash flow, supported by $3.2 billion in operating cash flow. This represented a strong rebound from the $150 million cash outflow reported in last year’s Q2. Lockheed Martin’s total backlog climbed to a record $230 billion, helped by major contracts such as expanded THAAD interceptor production and a $10.5 billion logistics agreement with U.S. Special Operations Command. “These awards are less about any single program than about what they were building in aggregate. Together, they strengthen the nation's production base, adding resilience along with more manufacturing capacity, more sources of supply and greater surge capability, all at a time when these very attributes have become a strategic imperative for the country,” said Lockheed’s CEO, James Taiclet, at the Q2 earnings call. Lockheed Martin stock edged 0.2% lower overnight, heading into Friday. The stock has climbed over 11% so far this week. The U.S. defense industry is entering a period of heightened investor interest following the House passage of a proposed $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2027 on Wednesday. The legislation reinforces expectations that military funding will remain a durable priority despite broader debates over federal spending. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around RTX remained in ‘extremely bullish’ territory. Sentiment around LMT improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ territory the previous day. A user said, “Lockheed $LMT – co-manufacturer of F22 Raptor - Stock Soars. Defense Is a Bipartisan Issue.” Another user said, “It hasn't been a great year since February for this sector, but now there is new funding coming in and other factors -- this sector is going to see some love.” So far this year, RTX and LMT stocks have gained 14% and 17%, respectively. (SEZL) is headed for its worst weekly decline since March this year, but it barely puts a dent in the company’s 2026 performance. Management also raised its full-year adjusted net income guidance to $180 million and projected 30% to 35% revenue growth for 2026, reinforcing confidence in the company's growth trajectory. Meanwhile, user growth and engagement also stayed strong through the year. Active subscribers surged 48.4% in Q1 year-on-year to 714,000, while Monthly On-Demand Users and Subscribers rose 34.8% to 887,000. Active consumers increased 13.6% to 3.1 million. Customer engagement also strengthened, with average quarterly purchase frequency reaching a record 7.1 transactions per user, up from 6.1 a year earlier. Repeat customers accounted for 97% of all platform orders, total transactions climbed 35.8% to 9.9 million and Gross Merchandise Volume went up by 37.3% to $1.1 billion. (TMUS) stock is headed toward its worst week in six years after mixed fiscal second-quarter (Q2) results, yet Goldman Sachs reiterated its ‘Buy’ rating, citing improving cash flow and 35% upside potential. T-Mobile stock fell over 10% on Thursday as investors looked past better-than-expected Q2 earnings and a higher full-year cash flow forecast, instead worrying that higher-priced plans could slow subscriber growth in the coming months. Goldman Sachs increased its price target for T-Mobile to $230 from $224 while citing continued operational strength and growth opportunities, implying a 35% upside to the stock’s last price. T-Mobile added 277,000 postpaid accounts during Q2, reflecting healthy demand across both mobile phone and broadband services. Goldman Sachs said the company continues to show solid customer momentum, though it expects account additions to moderate to roughly 250,000 in Q3 as some customers react to recent pricing changes. Goldman Sachs said investors may be concerned about T-Mobile’s unchanged 2026 forecast and weaker Q3 expectations, but the firm remains positive on the company’s future growth prospects, citing higher revenue per customer and greater room to add subscribers. Speaking during the Q2 earnings call, T-Mobile US CFO Peter Osvaldik reassured investors that it still expects healthy customer growth for the full year, even as he acknowledged that changes to its pricing strategy will likely weigh on subscriber additions during Q3. “As part of our full year plan and guidance, we anticipated our Q3 rate plan modernization would result in a temporary elevated account churn profile and expect Q3 net postpaid account additions to be approximately 250,000.” Osvaldik said that the expected increase in churn should have a smaller effect on postpaid phone customers because the pricing changes are primarily concentrated among accounts with fewer wireless lines. That distinction suggests the company expects its larger customer relationships to remain relatively stable throughout the transition. He added that the company continues to expect postpaid net account additions of between 950,000 and 1.05 million for 2026. Management said the forecast reflects confidence in the underlying strength of the business despite near-term headwinds tied to its pricing changes. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock jumped to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ territory the previous day, with a 450% increase in message volume over the past week. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ) and Charter Communications Inc. (CHTR) are set to report their second-quarter (Q2) earnings results on Friday. The telecom giants are facing a tight market, shaped by fixed wireless expansion, aggressive fiber footprints, and AI-driven cost controls. Additionally, SpaceX’s (SPCX) aggressive push into the communications sector by transforming Starlink into a comprehensive telecom platform is adding additional pressure. The New York-based American telecommunications giant is expected to post about a 2% increase in Q2 revenue expected to $35.11 billion from $34.5 billion in the previous comparable quarter, according to Fiscal.ai data. Meanwhile, earnings per share are expected to grow about 4% from $1.22 to $1.27 in the quarter. Verizon trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 8.8x, comparatively lower than AT&T Inc.’s (T) 9.5x multiple and T-Mobile US Inc.’s (TMUS) 13.7x. However, Charter’s forward P/E ratio is significantly lower, trading at a multiple of 2.9x. Despite Verizon’s lower valuation multiple, some Wall Street analysts are wary of the company’s strategy, believing that aggressive cost-cutting alone may not be enough to reignite growth. Earlier this month, reports suggested that Verizon is cutting about 3,000 positions at its corporate-owned retail stores by transitioning 274 locations to independent ownership. Meanwhile, SpaceX’s plans to transform Starlink into a mainstream consumer mobile service is also adding additional pressure. Wall Street analysts are on the fence about Verizon, with 15 out of 26 analysts covering the stock rating it a ‘Hold,’ as per latest data from Koyfin. The rest rate it a ‘Buy.’ However, the average 12-month price target of $51.12 implies an upside of about 16.66% from the stock’s last close. Charter is expected to post about a 2% decline in Q2 revenue from $13.766 billion in 2025 to $13.51 billion this quarter, as per Fiscal.ai data. However, analysts expect an increase of about 13% in earnings per share in the quarter, forecast to come in at $10.41 versus $9.18 in the previous comparable quarter. Meanwhile, reports from last month suggested that Charter has held discussions with Elon Musk's aerospace company over a potential consumer mobile partnership. The talks reportedly involve Charter routing a portion of SpaceX's mobile traffic through its terrestrial broadband network, though neither company has confirmed the discussions so far. Wall Street analysts have a 12-month average price target of $210.32 on CHTR shares, implying an upside of more than 66% from its last close. Of the 21 analysts covering the stock, only five have a ‘Buy’ rating, while 11 have a ‘Hold’ rating on the company. The rest rate it ‘Sell’ or lower. Meanwhile, retail sentiment around CHTR stock was also ‘bearish’ amid a 90% increase in message volumes. Both tickers were trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing. One user said, “$VZ It's gonna be a good day tomorrow!” Another user said, “$VZ $TMUS down -9.60% despite a neutral good earnings. $VZ will follow - good position building opportunity tomorrow.  Happy Friday is might be.” A third user said, “$CHTR It will take a few quarters but I think the turn around starts now. Cable is not going away for a while and the enhancements to existing infrastructure will get the company through a few more years until they start thinking more seriously about fiber. Plus the rural expansion makes them an attractive partner to sat companies or a good potential merger candidate for other telcos.” VZ stock has gained about 8% in 2026, while CHTR stock has declined more than 39%. title: Chevron (CVX) On Middle East Tensions, But Is The Valuation Case Still There? - Sahm
content: Chevron (CVX) On Middle East Tensions, But Is The Valuation Case Still There? Chevron (CVX) is back in focus as rising Middle East tensions and the closure of key shipping routes lift oil prices, while the company’s long dividend track record and favorable analyst coverage support investor interest. Recent Middle East tensions and higher oil prices have coincided with a strong run in Chevron, with the stock at $194.79 and a 24.95% year to date share price return, alongside a 31.07% 1 year total shareholder return. This suggests that momentum has been building rather than fading as investors reassess both cash flow prospects and risk. If you are looking beyond Chevron while energy markets stay in focus, this could be a good moment to scan other power grid and infrastructure opportunities via our 35 power grid technology and infrastructure stocks Chemical and geopolitical tailwinds have pushed Chevron close to $195, yet analyst targets sit higher and some intrinsic value models point to an even wider gap. Where does a reasonable fair value range really sit as this move settles in? Chevron’s most followed narrative puts fair value at $216.04 per share, above the recent $194.79 close, which frames the current move as still leaving a gap. Record production growth, especially in the Permian and from the Hess acquisition (Guyana, Bakken), positions Chevron to meet the rising energy demand from global population growth and emerging markets, supporting higher baseline revenues and longer-term cash generation. Want to see why this narrative places Chevron’s valuation above today’s price? It focuses on steady revenue expansion, rising margins and a richer future earnings multiple. The mix underpinning that $216.04 fair value may surprise you. However, this Chevron narrative could be challenged if long term oil demand weakens faster than expected or if large upstream projects face delays and cost overruns. While the popular narrative frames Chevron as undervalued around $194.79 versus a $216.04 fair value, the current 35x P/E tells a different story. That multiple sits well above the US Oil and Gas industry at 14.3x and also above a 29.6x fair ratio estimate, which points to richer pricing and less room for error if expectations shift. For investors weighing up Chevron, the question is whether this premium reflects durable strength or leaves limited cushion if the story changes. It also raises how comfortable you are paying above both industry and fair ratio levels for the stock.
